title: Role of Occupational Therapy for Persons Experiencing Long COVID: A Rapid Review
authors: Kang AK, Le Huynh T, Tran T, Mofina A
summary: This rapid review searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL (January 2020–December 2024) and included 21 articles describing occupational therapy for adults and older adults with long COVID. The occupational therapy role centered on addressing fatigue, weakness, and cognitive impairments that limit daily occupational performance. Interventions were delivered mostly in inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation settings and included ADL/IADL retraining, cognitive rehabilitation, physical and breathing exercises, energy conservation and fatigue management education, return-to-work planning, and psychosocial support. Most studies described interprofessional, team-based care rather than occupational therapy-specific interventions studied in isolation, and only 17 of 21 articles met at least 80% of relevant JBI critical appraisal criteria.
forPatients: If you're dealing with long COVID symptoms like fatigue, brain fog, or trouble managing daily tasks, occupational therapy can help. This review found that OT commonly focuses on teaching energy conservation and pacing strategies, retraining everyday activities like self-care and household tasks, and supporting a safe return to work. Programs such as Fatigue and Activity Management Education (FAME-PC) and Energy Management Education (EME) showed improvements in fatigue, function, and quality of life. Care is often delivered by a team of providers (not OT alone), in person or increasingly through telehealth.
forPhysio: This rapid review of 21 studies maps the current landscape of OT practice for long COVID across the care continuum, though the majority of included studies were pilot, feasibility, or case-level designs with team-based (not OT-isolated) interventions, limiting causal claims about OT-specific effects. Clinically, the strongest signal is for energy conservation/fatigue management education (e.g., FAME-PC, EME) and functional retraining of ADLs/IADLs, with return-to-work support as a recurring, valued OT contribution. Cognitive and psychosocial interventions were reported far less often despite high rates of brain fog, anxiety, and depression in this population — representing a clear gap and opportunity for OT-led intervention and outcome measurement. Long-COVID-specific outcome measures remain scarce (only the C19-YRS and Symptom Burden Questionnaire for Long COVID were identified), so most clinicians are borrowing tools validated in other conditions (e.g., MFIS, FIM, Lawton IADL Scale). Telerehabilitation is an emerging, feasible delivery model but has limitations for rapport-building and hands-on assessment.
keyFindings: 17 of 21 included articles described a distinct occupational therapy role in long COVID care, most often within interprofessional, team-based rehabilitation rather than isolated OT-only interventions

Physical interventions (ADL/IADL retraining, exercise, energy and fatigue management) were the most common OT focus, followed by patient education on sleep hygiene, symptom management, and caregiver education
Occupational therapy-led fatigue/energy management programs (FAME-PC, EME) showed statistically significant improvements in fatigue impact, self-efficacy, and health-related quality of life
Cognitive and psychosocial interventions were reported far less frequently than physical interventions, despite long COVID's high prevalence of brain fog, anxiety, and depression

Only two long COVID-specific assessment tools (C19-YRS and the Symptom Burden Questionnaire for Long COVID) were used across the 21 studies; most measures were borrowed from other conditions with similar symptom profiles
